cases.working_notes: Abstract links residual coding to single-pass generation; Results contrasts standalone and sequential completion to locate the advantage beyond basic manipulation success. Timing measures action inference, not end-to-end execution; faster inference is not isolated as the cause of higher success. Retain the modified diffusion comparator and closed-loop control. Report descriptive trial counts without significance claims. Table 3's condition labels conflict with its methods, and extracted entropy labels are ambiguous; use Table 7 timings and qualitative diversity. Ablation figure labels also appear inconsistent with the stated task names, so do not quote their task-specific values.
cases.abstract: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) model multimodal behavior using learned latent action tokens rather than clustering actions directly. Residual quantization combines coarse codes with finer corrections; a transformer predicts these codes from observation histories, optionally conditioned on goals, and an offset refines decoded actions. Action or action-chunk generation takes one forward pass, avoiding the iterative denoising used by diffusion policies. Across simulated manipulation and locomotion tasks, VQ-BeT combines competitive task performance with diverse behavior, although diffusion policies perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a real mobile manipulator, standalone-task success is similar to a modified transformer diffusion policy (47/50 versus 45/50), whereas two-task completion reaches 19/30 versus 11/30. For each of four longer tasks, VQ-BeT also achieves at least three times the baseline's final success count. With all policies executed fully closed-loop, mean inference on an RTX A4000 is 18.06 ms versus 573.49 ms for the diffusion baseline. The real-robot comparison couples higher sequence-completion rates with lower action-generation time under per-step feedback.
cases.results: VQ-BeT's advantage on the mobile manipulator is larger for task sequences than for standalone operations. It completes 47 of 50 standalone trials, compared with 45 of 50 for a modified DiffusionPolicy-T, but succeeds in 19 of 30 two-task trials versus 11 of 30. Across four longer tasks, each evaluated in ten trials, VQ-BeT's final success count is at least three times the baseline's. The larger sequence-completion gap places the benefit beyond isolated manipulation success; VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both possible orders. All policies run fully closed-loop because receding-horizon execution fails on this robot's imprecise controller. In this setting, mean inference on an RTX A4000 is 18.06 ms for VQ-BeT and 573.49 ms for DiffusionPolicy-T. Thus, the improved sequence-completion rates accompany substantially shorter action-generation times when feedback is incorporated at every step.

cases.working_notes: Abstract explains why using the same hybrid action rule in interaction and TD targets differs from actor regularization; ablations support both proposal roles beyond dropout. Results uses Hang to distinguish improvement over imitation from RL baselines that finish below it, and Drawer to expose the fixed-budget success gap. Hang's 85% versus 65% is a 20-percentage-point gain. Use Table I's 15% for early-stop RFT despite the prose saying below 15%. Hardware scores are 20-trial evaluations, not training-curve averages or independent training seeds. Preserve manual resets and avoid claims of autonomous deployment or globally optimal action selection.
cases.abstract: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a separately trained imitation policy to guide sparse-reward robot learning without imposing an imitation loss on the RL actor. A critic selects the higher-valued imitation or RL action both during interaction and when constructing temporal-difference targets, aligning bootstrapping with the hybrid interaction policy. Keeping the policies separate permits different imitation and RL encoders; actor dropout and a shallow vision-transformer critic further improve pixel-based learning. IBRL matches regularized fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks and outperforms fine-tuning and demonstration oversampling on harder Robomimic tasks. With 50 demonstrations, it solves pixel-based Square within 500,000 interaction steps, while these baselines remain below 60% success. On real-robot cloth hanging, 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online steps yield 85% success over 20 evaluations, versus 65% for imitation, 35% for fine-tuning, and 15% for oversampling. Hardware training uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. Removing either imitation proposal degrades performance even with actor dropout, supporting the contribution of imitation in both interaction and value-target computation.
cases.results: On cloth hanging, IBRL improves on the imitation reference, whereas regularized fine-tuning (RFT) and demonstration oversampling (RLPD) achieve lower success than that reference. Given 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, compared with 65% for behavior cloning, 35% for RFT, and 15% for RLPD. Each method is evaluated in 20 trials with the same initial conditions. The 20-percentage-point gain over behavior cloning distinguishes online policy improvement from simply maintaining the imitation policy's initial performance. Drawer provides a complementary comparison of interaction efficiency: with 30 demonstrations, IBRL reaches 100% success at the 10,000-step checkpoint, while RFT reaches 15% and RLPD 0%, again in 20 evaluations. These hardware results use sparse binary success rewards and manual resets between training episodes.
